description:
We are four mathematics students from Yıldız Technical University who share one belief: questions usually left to intuition can be measured, tested and proven. Each of us brings a different strength, from software and research to mathematical methods and data analysis, and we work as one team where every idea is challenged and improved together.

Orbitrary is where that belief met space exploration: using topology and open NASA data, it reads the shape of Earth to find the Moon and Mars.
summary: Earth sites are used to prepare crews and rovers for missions to the Moon and Mars, and NASA has selected such sites case by case. In this project, a method and an open website were built to search for these sites systematically. All 346,064 land windows of 20 × 20 km on Earth are compared with a chosen lunar or martian location in eight categories derived from open orbital data: topography, terrain shape, geology, mineralogy, thermal behaviour, water ice, dust and illumination. Each category is converted into a percentile among Earth's land windows, which are then combined into one score for each of five mission types, with physical requirements such as a slope limit for rover tests. The Earth sites that NASA used for training ranked above chance for the targets they were used for (p = 0.044), while rainforest and cropland control windows ranked at the bottom. Results are published for 26 targets, including the nine Artemis III candidate regions (Oct 2024; first landing now planned as Artemis IV), and for every location on the Moon and Mars. For each match, the website shows in which categories it resembles the target and in which it does not.
details:
What the project does: A user selects a location on the Moon or Mars, either by clicking on a 3D globe or by choosing one of 26 predefined targets, and selects a mission type: General, Mobility test, Geology, Ice & resources or Astrobiology. The website returns the Earth locations that are most similar to the selected location for that mission, shows them on a map, and explains each result category by category.

How it works: All three bodies are divided into the same 20 × 20 km windows with 500 m cells. Each window is described in eight categories. Terrain is described by the distributions of slope, ruggedness and curvature, which are compared with the Wasserstein distance, and by the arrangement of basins and peaks, which is compared with persistent homology. Quantities with different physical ranges on different bodies, such as temperature, ice indicators and illumination, are compared through their rank within their own body: "among the coldest 5% of the Moon" is compared with "among the coldest 5% of Earth". Each category distance is converted into a percentile among Earth's land windows, so a value of 0.95 means that the Earth window is closer to the target than 95% of Earth's land. The percentiles are combined with mission weights. Physical gates remove locations where a mission cannot be attempted, for example windows that are too steep for a rover test or without permafrost for an ice test. For the 26 targets, every one of the 346,064 land windows was scored. For the click map of the whole Moon (94,864 windows) and Mars (360,654 windows), results were computed in advance with a faster terrain prefilter, because the website runs without a server.

Validation: All weights, thresholds and test pairs were fixed before any result was computed. Eleven documented NASA training sites, such as the Apollo geology-training sites and the JETT field-test sites, were scored for their own targets. They ranked above chance (p = 0.044): the median site scored higher than 75.6% of Earth's land windows, and higher than 86.6% for the eight sites that meet the mission requirement. Twenty-two rainforest and cropland windows chosen in advance ranked at the bottom. With only 11 documented pairs, the 95% interval of the discrimination test still includes chance, and this limit is stated on the website and in the paper.

Benefits and intended impact: Mission planners and field-test teams get a ranked list of candidate sites for any lunar or martian location, with the reason for each match and the categories in which it differs from the target. All 336 top-3 windows of the 26 targets lie more than 100 km from every site in the project's list of documented analog sites, so the results also propose new candidate regions for field checks. Every result reports missing data and the side on which data are missing, so that a high score is not mistaken for a complete comparison.

Tools, languages and data: Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, GDAL, rasterio, GeoPandas and shapely; GUDHI for persistent homology; earthaccess for NASA Earthdata downloads; matplotlib for figures. The website uses HTML and JavaScript with three.js for the globes and Leaflet for the maps, and is hosted on GitHub Pages. The computation ran on one Windows 11 workstation. The project uses 24 open datasets, including MODIS, ASTER, LRO LOLA and Diviner, Lunar Prospector, MGS MOLA and TES, and Mars Odyssey data. All code is open and every random step uses a fixed seed, so the results can be reproduced.

What is new: The project compares locations on three bodies across Earth's whole land surface, with a separate result for each mission type and a percentile reading that is the same in every category. Terrain shape is compared with persistent homology in addition to classic terrain parameters. A worst-case bound states when elevation errors cannot change the terrain similarities.

Factors the team considered: Data from different instruments are not physically equivalent, so they are compared by rank and not by value. Missing data are not set to zero; they are removed from the score and reported. Some known analog sites that are vegetated today, such as the Ries and Sudbury impact structures, fail the Geology requirement of bare rock. Windows of 20 km cannot resolve features of a few kilometres, and a high score means similarity in the measured categories, not environmental equivalence. The results are candidates for field work, not confirmed analogs.

Code and text editing were assisted by Claude (Anthropic). Problem interpretation, the method, thresholds and all decisions are the team's own. All outputs were verified with automated tests. Claude was used as a coding, editing and literature-search assistant; every reference was opened and checked by a team member. No SI-generated images, audio or video are included in the website, video or article.
